The study employs a randomized controlled trial comparing two velocity loss thresholds (VL10 vs. VL30) in resistance training. The core duality lies in how these thresholds shape neuromuscular adaptation: VL10 prioritizes velocity preservation, leading to enhanced explosive performance metrics such as standing long jump (SLJ) and sprint times (T30), while VL30 emphasizes higher repetition volumes, favoring maximal strength gains (1RM). This dualism arises from differing fatigue dynamics—lower thresholds maintain higher mean propulsive velocities, promoting fast-twitch fiber recruitment and power output, whereas higher thresholds induce greater metabolic stress and neural drive, enhancing strength. The mixed-design ANOVA allows for capturing group-by-time interactions, revealing non-uniform responses across performance domains. For instance, VL10 shows superior improvement in SLJ and T30 (p=0.031, p=0.006 respectively), indicating its specificity for high-velocity tasks. Conversely, VL30 excels in 1RM gains, suggesting it better stimulates strength-related adaptations. These findings align with theoretical frameworks where velocity-based training (VBT) leverages neuromuscular fatigue markers to optimize training prescriptions. The mathematical structure reflects a trade-off between velocity and volume, modeled as a function of set termination criteria. In GSI, this manifests as a Bayesian update on performance likelihood given threshold inputs. In GSE, it translates into state transitions governed by velocity loss dynamics.
